blocks.prompt: The Skunk That Warns You First
blocks.text: A skunk has a warning to give you, and it gives it in order. First it stamps its front feet on the ground. Then it hisses. Then it lifts its fluffy tail straight up. All of that means the same thing. Please go away. A skunk only sprays when nothing else has worked. It can spray about six times, and then it has to wait about ten days to make more. Spray is costly for a skunk. That is why its black and white stripes are so easy to see. The stripes say: you already know who I am.

blocks.prompt: The Warning Comes First
blocks.text: A skunk would rather not spray you. That sounds strange, but the reason is really just counting. A skunk carries only about six sprays in two small glands under its tail. Once those are gone, it needs roughly ten days to make more. For those ten days it has almost nothing to defend itself with. So a skunk spends a lot of effort making sure it never has to spray at all. That is what the stripes are for. Black and white is the easiest pattern to see in the dark, and it works like a sign that says you have met me before. If the sign does not work, the skunk adds a warning dance. It stamps its front feet hard on the ground. It hisses. It raises its tail. A spotted skunk will even stand up on its front paws like a gymnast, tail waving overhead. Every part of that show is a request. Leave. Only when the request is ignored does the skunk turn around and take aim.

blocks.prompt: An Honest Threat
blocks.text: A skunk is a small animal with a slow walk, weak eyesight, and no real weapons. It cannot outrun a coyote. It cannot fight a bobcat. What it has instead is a chemistry set: two glands beside its tail that hold an oily yellow liquid made of sulfur compounds called thiols. A skunk can fire that liquid about ten feet and aim it at a face. The smell clings to fur and skin for days, and any animal that gets a faceful remembers it for the rest of its life. That memory is the whole point. A skunk carries only about six sprays, and rebuilding the supply takes roughly ten days. A skunk that empties its glands is a skunk with no defense at all. So the animal invests everything in not needing to spray. Its black and white pattern is not camouflage, which would hide it. It is the opposite of camouflage. Scientists call bold warning coloration aposematism, and it works because it is memorable. The stripes are a claim, and the claim is honest: bother me and you will regret it. Then come the warnings. Foot stamping. Hissing. The tail going up like a flag. Spotted skunks add a handstand, walking forward on their front paws with the tail fanned overhead, which is somehow both ridiculous and effective. Most predators have learned to read all of it and simply leave. The exception is the great horned owl, which hunts skunks regularly. An owl has a poor sense of smell, so the threat means almost nothing to it. A warning only works on someone who can understand it.

blocks.prompt: The Economics of a Bad Smell
blocks.text: Think of a skunk's spray as money in a very small bank account. Two glands beside the tail hold enough for roughly six discharges. Spend them all and the account is empty for about ten days while the body slowly refills it. During that stretch the skunk is a slow, half blind, ordinary little animal in a forest full of coyotes. Seen that way, every spray is a small catastrophe, and the skunk's entire behavior makes sense as an effort to avoid spending anything at all. Everything you notice about a skunk is advertising. The black and white pattern is not an accident of fashion. It is the loudest signal an animal can wear at night, when most of its predators hunt, and biologists call this kind of deliberate visibility aposematism. Camouflage says do not find me. Aposematism says find me, look closely, and remember. If a predator recognizes the pattern from a distance and turns away, the skunk has defended itself for free. The signal only works because it is backed by something real. The liquid in those glands is built from thiols, sulfur compounds so strong that a human nose can detect them at a few parts per billion. They cling to fur and skin, they burn the eyes, and a fresh spray can be smelled a mile away in the right wind. An animal that learns this lesson does not need to learn it twice. If the pattern fails, the skunk escalates rather than fires. It stamps its front feet in a rapid drum roll. It hisses and puffs. It hoists its tail. A spotted skunk rears into a handstand and walks toward the threat on its front paws, tail spread like a flag. Only when the whole performance is ignored does the skunk pivot, aim over its shoulder, and spend the money. There is a footnote worth knowing. People have been dunking sprayed dogs in tomato juice for generations, and it does not work. It only overwhelms your nose, which is a different thing from removing the smell. In 1993 a chemist named Paul Krebaum published a mixture of hydrogen peroxide, baking soda, and dish soap that actually oxidizes the thiols into compounds with no smell at all. The problem was never bad enough scrubbing. It was chemistry.

blocks.prompt: The Honest Signal: Why a Skunk Almost Never Sprays
blocks.text: The strangest fact about skunks is how rarely they use the thing they are famous for. A striped skunk carries roughly six discharges in two glands beside its tail, and once those are spent the body needs about ten days to rebuild the supply. For those ten days the animal is what it always was underneath: slow, nearsighted, and small, wandering a landscape that contains coyotes, bobcats, and foxes. Every spray is therefore expensive, and almost everything a skunk does is an attempt to avoid paying. Start with the coat. Black and white is the most conspicuous pattern an animal can wear at night, which is precisely when a skunk is out and precisely when its predators are hunting. This is not a design flaw. Biologists call it aposematism: advertising rather than hiding. Camouflage is a request not to be noticed. Aposematism is a demand to be noticed, examined, and filed away in memory. A coyote that recognizes the pattern from thirty feet and changes direction has just been defeated by a skunk that did nothing at all. That is the cheapest possible victory, and it is the one the skunk is playing for. The signal works only because it is not a bluff. The fluid in those glands is built from thiols, sulfur compounds that the human nose registers at a few parts per billion. It is oily, so it grips fur. It stings the eyes. And it carries a genuinely clever twist: alongside the thiols are compounds called thioacetates, which have little smell on their own but break down in water and release fresh thiols. This is why washing a sprayed dog can make the problem worse, and why the animal can still reek weeks later on a humid morning. The skunk is not just delivering a punishment. It is delivering a punishment with a timer on it. Between the coat and the fluid sits the part most people never see, because most people never get close enough. A skunk escalates in stages. It drums its front feet against the ground in a fast, unmistakable rhythm. It hisses and puffs its fur. It lifts its tail. A spotted skunk goes further and rears into a handstand, advancing on its front paws with its tail spread overhead, an act that looks comic and is not. Every stage is a chance for the intruder to leave, and the skunk offers all of them before it turns and aims. There is exactly one predator that treats the whole performance as noise. The great horned owl hunts skunks routinely, because an owl has almost no sense of smell. The threat is real, the warning is honest, and the owl simply cannot read the message. A signal is worthless to an audience that lacks the sense to receive it. Two further notes for the curious. Skunks were long filed alongside weasels and badgers in the family Mustelidae, until genetic work in the 1990s showed they had diverged far earlier than the resemblance suggested, and they were moved into a family of their own, Mephitidae. And in 1993 a chemist named Paul Krebaum published the mixture that actually works on a sprayed dog: hydrogen peroxide, baking soda, and dish soap, which oxidize the thiols into odorless compounds. Tomato juice, the folk remedy of a century, does nothing but exhaust your nose. Both notes point the same way. The skunk had been telling the truth the entire time. We were the ones who kept getting it wrong.
